historia.intro: Fifty levels that tighten step by step: board, mines, opponents and clock.

1.texto: Small boards, an opponent that clicks almost blindly and, for the first five levels, no clock at all.

2.texto: The board grows, the mines pack together and the clock is running. Halfway through, a third player sits down.

3.texto: Opponents that really deduce, cross-referencing one number with another, and fewer seconds per turn each level.

4.texto: Big boards and, in the second half, four players fighting over the same mines.

5.texto: The hardest of the lot: level 5 opponents, the densest boards and six seconds per turn at the end.

ayuda.intro: The rules of MineHunt, exactly as the game applies them right now.

objetivo.texto: This is minesweeper turned around: you do not avoid mines, you hunt them. Each click uncovers a single cell, which either hides a mine (scored on your board) or tells you how many mines surround it. Most mines found wins.

turnos.texto: Find a mine and you keep the turn, chaining as many turns as mines you hit in a row. The moment you miss, the turn passes to the next player.

reloj.texto: If the game has a time limit per turn, the bar at the top drains and turns red in the final seconds. Run out and you lose the turn without playing, leaving the board untouched. The clock restarts with every click, including when you keep the turn.

onda.texto: Spend it on an empty cell and it drags every connected one. In the browser, right-clicking a cell fires it there directly, without touching this button; on mobile, tapping the same cell twice does the same. On a numbered cell only that cell is revealed and the shockwave is wasted; on a mine, the mine is scored and it is spent anyway.

rendirse.texto: You can leave the game on your turn and, if you are the only human at the table, while the bots think too. You are out: no more turns come your way, your mines stop counting and you can no longer win, but you still get to watch how it ends. If your surrender leaves a single player standing, the game ends there and that player wins, so in two-player games surrendering is also the way out.

fin.texto: The game runs until the last mine is uncovered, even if the result was settled long before. The other way to end it is everyone surrendering but one: that player wins, whatever their score. If the last mine leaves a tie at the top, there is no winner. However it ends, the whole board is uncovered afterwards: you get to see where the remaining mines were and what every square was hiding.

bots.texto: Every AI seat plays at its own level, from 1 (clicks blindly) to 5 (deduces, weighs probabilities and picks where to spend the shockwave). They take between 0 and 2 seconds before moving, so you can see them think.

historia.texto: Fifty levels under the same rules, with the difficulty climbing four ways at once: a bigger board, more mines, smarter (and more numerous) opponents and less time per turn. You only move forward by winning: lose and you replay the level, but you never lose what you had already cleared. Progress is saved on this device.

acerca.que_es: MineHunt is minesweeper inverted: mines are not avoided here, they are hunted. Whoever finds the most wins. Find one and you keep playing; miss and you hand over the turn. The shockwave clears half an area at once if you spend it in the right place.
acerca.modos: Play solo against bots, level by level in Story Mode, or online with up to four players.

autoria.texto: A game by Capicua, developed by José Luis Bautista.
